# Tab: Overview # Project Atlas: Q3 delivery plan ## Northwind Labs · Platform team · revision for the steering review # Summary Project Atlas replaces the three regional order pipelines with one event-driven service that every storefront can call. The current pipelines were written at different times, by different teams, against different assumptions about stock, payment and fraud checks, and the cost of keeping them aligned has grown with every new market. The goal for this quarter is a production launch in two regions, with the third following once the migration tooling has been exercised on real traffic. This document is the working plan: it lists the goals, the milestones and their owners, the budget, and the risks we already know about. Comments are welcome in the margin; decisions are recorded in the Decisions log tab. The plan was reviewed with [Ana Souza](mailto:ana.souza@example.com) (engineering lead) and [Marcus Lee](mailto:marcus.lee@example.org) (product) on Oct 28, 2026. The launch checklist lives in [Atlas launch checklist](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Sheet0Atlas0Launch0Checklist0Example000/edit) and is the source of truth for go/no-go items. Atlas was first proposed in the platform strategy memo[^1] and funded in the spring planning cycle. Since then the scope has narrowed: the loyalty integration and the marketplace sellers moved to a later phase, so the first release only covers first-party orders. The narrower scope is what makes a single-quarter launch realistic. # Goals We will consider the quarter a success when all of the following hold at the end of September: - One order service handles every first-party order in the north and south regions. - Peak traffic is served without manual scaling. - Black-friday load test at three times last year's peak. - Failover between zones takes less than two minutes. - The legacy pipelines in those regions are read-only and scheduled for deletion. - Order latency at the 99th percentile stays under 400 ms, measured at the storefront edge as described in the [latency SLO runbook](https://wiki.example.com/platform/slo/order-latency). - Support tickets about missing or duplicated orders drop below the pre-launch baseline. Non-goals for this quarter are just as important. We are not changing the storefront APIs, we are not migrating historical orders older than eighteen months, and we are not replacing the fraud vendor. Each of these came up during planning and each would have pushed the launch out by at least a month. If one of them becomes urgent, it gets its own plan and its own owner rather than being folded into Atlas. # Milestones The work is sequenced so that each milestone can ship on its own and be rolled back without touching the others. 1. Shadow traffic 1. Mirror north-region orders to Atlas and compare outcomes. 2. Fix every divergence above 0.1% before moving on. 1. Triage divergences daily. 2. Publish the comparison dashboard. 2. Canary in the north region 1. Route 5% of orders, then 25%, then 50%, one step per week. 3. Full launch in north and south 4. Read-only legacy pipelines | Milestone | Owner | Target date | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Shadow traffic | [Priya Raman](mailto:priya.raman@example.com) | Jul 14 | Done | | Canary (north) | [Tomás Ferreira](mailto:tomas.ferreira@example.com) | Aug 4 | In progress | | Full launch | Ana Souza | Sep 1 | Not started
Blocked on capacity review | | Legacy read-only | Marcus Lee | Sep 22 | Not started \| pending | Dates in the table are commitments, not estimates: a slip of more than a week is raised in the weekly steering review, with a proposal, rather than discovered at the end of the quarter. The architecture diagram below shows the target state once the full launch milestone is complete. ![Diagram: storefronts publish order events to the Atlas order service, which calls payments, fraud and fulfilment.]() Figure 1. Target architecture: storefronts publish order events; Atlas owns validation, payment and fulfilment hand-off. # Owners and contacts Escalations go to the on-call engineer first, then to the milestone owner. On-call rota: Team channel: #atlas-launch For anything about scope or priorities, talk to [Marcus Lee](mailto:marcus.lee@example.org); for anything about the technical design, [Ana Souza](mailto:ana.souza@example.com). Vendor questions (payments, fraud) go through procurement and are tracked in the vendor sheet. # Budget The approved budget covers infrastructure for both regions and one contractor for the migration tooling. Cloud spend is estimated with the usual capacity formula [equation], where peak orders per second is taken from last year's busiest hour. The estimate below includes a 20% contingency. | Item | Q3 estimate | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Compute (two regions) | $84,000 | Reserved instances from August | | Managed queue and storage | $21,500 | | | Migration contractor | $48,000 | Twelve weeks | | Contingency (20%) | $30,700 | Released after launch | --- Earlier versions of this plan are linked from the [project page](https://wiki.example.com/platform/atlas?utm_source=docs). See also the risk register in the Engineering plan tab. [^1]: Platform strategy memo, March 2026, section 4 (“One order path”). # Tab: Overview / Timeline # Timeline ### Week 27 Shadow traffic enabled for the north region. The comparison job runs every hour and posts divergences to the team channel. The first run found a rounding difference in tax totals for orders with more than twenty lines, which was fixed the same day. ### Week 29 Divergence rate below 0.1% for five consecutive days. Load test at two times last year's peak passed; the queue consumer needed one extra partition to keep lag under thirty seconds. ### Week 31 Canary at 5% of north-region orders. Two incidents, both caused by a stale feature flag in one storefront; neither lost an order, and the flag cleanup is now part of the release checklist. ### Week 32 Canary at 25%. Payment authorisation latency improved by 18% compared with the legacy path because Atlas reuses connections to the payment gateway. ### Week 33 Canary at 50%. Capacity review for the south region scheduled; the full-launch date depends on its outcome. # Tab: Engineering plan # Engineering plan This tab describes how the order service is built and operated. It is written for the engineers on the team and for reviewers from security and finance, so it favours concrete decisions over background. Where a decision is still open it says so, with the owner who will close it. ## Architecture Storefronts publish an OrderPlaced event to a regional queue. The Atlas consumer validates the order against the catalogue snapshot, reserves stock, authorises the payment and hands the order to fulfilment. Each step writes its outcome to the order log before acknowledging the event, so a crash at any point is recovered by replaying the log rather than by reconciling three systems after the fact. The legacy pipelines did the same steps synchronously inside the storefront request, which is why a slow payment gateway used to show up as checkout timeouts. State lives in one regional database per region with a hot standby in a second zone. Cross-region traffic is limited to the catalogue snapshot, which is replicated every five minutes, and to the reporting export, which runs nightly. Nothing on the order path waits for another region. ## Testing strategy - Unit tests for every validation rule, generated from the rule table. - Contract tests against the payment and fraud sandboxes. - Replay tests: a day of production orders, anonymised, replayed against every release candidate. - Anonymisation removes names, addresses and card fingerprints.
